questions.prompt: A dictionary entry reads: "(noun) a place from which spacecraft take off and where they land". Which word does it define?
questions.explanation: The entry opens with "a place", so the word it defines must name a place and not a vehicle: a spaceport is to space travel what an airport is to flying — where the craft leaves from and where it comes back. A shuttle and a spaceship are the craft themselves, and a foothold names no place at all but a first strong position from which a company can make progress.

questions.prompt: Sami texts a friend: "I have finally finished ___ my application to the space camp." Which form completes the message?
questions.explanation: "Finish" belongs to the family of verbs followed directly by a verb in the -ing form, which gives "I have finally finished writing my application". The form with "to" copies the pattern of decide, hope and want, which is not the pattern of finish; the bare form leaves two verbs side by side with nothing joining them; and "written" is a past participle, so it would need an auxiliary such as have or be in front of it.

questions.prompt: In which line do the two words take negative prefixes spelt EXACTLY the same way?
questions.explanation: Legal and literate both begin with the letter l, and before an l the prefix is written il-, which gives illegal and illiterate. Every other line writes it differently: regular takes ir- but mature takes im-, obey takes dis- but welcome takes un-, and perfect takes im- while expensive takes in-. Remember that il-, im-, ir- and in- are one and the same prefix wearing four spellings, chosen by the first letter of the word: two words come out spelt alike only when their first letters call for the same spelling, as l and l do here, and as m, p and b all do for im-.

questions.prompt: A flight report says: "The pilot stopped to check the fuel gauge." What did the pilot do?

options.text: He had been checking it and gave that up.
He interrupted his work in order to check it.
He checked it every few minutes of the flight.
He finished checking it and went back to flying.

questions.explanation: After "stop", a to + infinitive gives the reason for stopping: the pilot broke off whatever he was doing so that he could look at the gauge — the checking begins, it does not end. The reading in which he had been checking and gave it up belongs to the other pattern, "stopped checking", where the -ing form names the activity that is cancelled. Nothing in the sentence says the check was repeated or already over.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you: "I have never left my town, and I am sure people everywhere behave exactly like my neighbours." Which proverb answers him?

options.text: He that travels far knows much.
The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only a page.
He who does not travel does not know the value of men.
Travelling teaches you the price of things.

questions.explanation: Your friend is not judging the size of the world but the people who live in it, and one proverb only is about people: whoever stays at home cannot know what men are worth, because he has met one kind of neighbour and no other. Praising the far traveller's knowledge, or comparing the world to a book of which he has read a single page, replies to another claim — that he has seen very little. And the saying about the price of things weighs what a journey costs, not what the men you meet on it are worth.
